references.text: [ref:Luk 18:4|Luke 18:4] repeats the description of the judge as one who "did not fear God and did not respect anyone," confirming his character as introduced in verse 2.
[ref:5 Mos 1:17|Deut 1:17] commands judges not to show partiality, for "the judgment belongs to God." The judge in Jesus' parable is a contrast to this ideal – he fears neither God nor people.
[ref:5 Mos 16:18-19|Deut 16:18-19] gives provisions that judges shall judge righteously and not pervert justice. The unjust judge in the parable is a contradiction to this divine ideal.

[ref:2 Krøn 19:6-7|2 Chron 19:6-7] exhorts judges to fear the Lord and judge righteously, for "with the Lord our God there is no injustice." The judge in Luke 18 lacks precisely this reverence for God.
[ref:Ordsp 1:7|Prov 1:7] states that "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge." The judge in the parable lacks this fundamental reverence for God, showing his moral decay.
[ref:Sal 36:2|Ps 36:2] describes the wicked one as saying: "There is no fear of God before his eyes." This parallels the description of the judge who did not fear God.
[ref:Rom 3:18|Rom 3:18] quotes from the Psalms: "There is no fear of God before their eyes." This description of humanity's sinful nature fits exactly with the characterization of the unjust judge.
[ref:Jes 1:17|Isa 1:17] urges to "help the fatherless, plead for the widow!" The judge in the parable is one who precisely fails to do this – until the widow forces him with her persistence.

[ref:Jes 10:1-2|Isa 10:1-2] pronounces woe on those who enact unjust laws and deny justice to the poor, robbing widows of their rights. The judge in the parable represents exactly this kind of injustice.

[ref:2 Mos 22:21-23|Exod 22:21-23] warns against oppressing widows and fatherless children, with a threat of God's wrath. The unjust judge's indifference toward the widow stands in sharp contrast to God's care for the vulnerable.
